claim: Let \(P(n)\) be the largest prime divisor of a composite integer \(n\ge 4\), and for \(k\ge1\) define \(\varphi_k(n)=n+k\) when \(n\) is prime and \(\varphi_k(n)=P(n)\) when \(n\) is composite. The exact cycles of lengths three and four are as follows. An exact three-cycle exists if and only if \(k=2^a-1\) for some \(a\ge1\) with \(2^a+1\) prime, and then the unique three-cycle is \((2,2^a+1,2^{a+1})\). Every exact four-cycle is of exactly one of two types: (I) a one-composite cycle, which occurs exactly when \(k=3^a-1\) with \(a\ge1\) and both \(3^a+2\) and \(2\cdot3^a+1\) prime, giving \((3,3^a+2,2\cdot3^a+1,3^{a+1})\); or (II) an alternating prime-composite cycle \((p,p+k,q,q+k)\), where \(p\ne q\) are primes and there is an integer \(t\ge1\) such that \(k=pqt-p-q\), \(pt-1\ge2\), \(qt-1\ge2\), \(P(pt-1)\le q\), and \(P(qt-1)\le p\). Conversely every parameter set satisfying the stated conditions gives the corresponding exact cycle. In particular, Bertrand's postulate gives infinitely many parameters with an exact four-cycle: for any odd prime \(p\), choose a prime \(q\) with \(p<q<2p\), put \(t=1\) and \(k=pq-p-q\).
integrity: The proof is symbolic and self-contained apart from standard primality terminology and Bertrand's postulate for the infinite period-four corollary. Computational checks are explicitly separated from proof.
scientific_limitations: Only exact periods 3 and 4 are classified.
Infinitely many period-3 parameters are not proved; this is equivalent to an infinitude question for Fermat primes.
Finite verification is regression evidence and is not used as an infinite proof.
title: Exact period-three and period-four cycles for \(\varphi_k\)
